name: Wool and merino clothes

card.summary: Fine sheep wool said to resist odour; the claim is popular but untested in the sources reviewed.
card.note: Wool can shrink with heat and agitation.

quick.overview:
Merino is a fine, soft wool used for clothing. People interested in smelling clean say it stays fresher than other fabrics.

No source reviewed here tests that.
quick.mechanism: Odour arises from bacteria acting on sweat; proponents believe wool limits this, though no reviewed source confirms it.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes heat and agitation shrink wool, and that a 2004 mulesing campaign led some retailers to drop Australian merino.[1][3]

lead: Merino is a fine, soft wool from the Merino sheep breed, widely used in sweaters, socks, T-shirts and base layers. In appearance and grooming discussions it is valued for how it feels and looks on the body: soft enough to wear against the skin, able to hold heat, and said to stay fresher-smelling between washes, which helps a person look and smell put together through a long day.

Wikipedia says the breed originated in the Iberian Peninsula in the High Middle Ages, and that its wool is generally under 24 microns in fibre diameter, graded from strong (23 to 24.5 microns) to ultra-fine (11.5 to 15 microns), with finer grades generally softer [1]. Wool in general readily absorbs moisture, up to nearly a third of its weight in water, and its crimped fibres trap air and retain heat [3].

Wearers say merino resists odour better than synthetics. Wikipedia's wool article says wool treated with lanolin is slightly antibacterial and resists odour build-up [3], and body odour is attributed to bacteria acting on skin secretions [2]. No study cited here directly compares merino with other fabrics for smell.

angle.text: People choose merino shirts, base layers and socks for comfort, temperature control and fewer odour problems, which supports a clean, comfortable presentation. Fine-grade merino also drapes and looks smooth, so it is used in tailored knitwear.

infobox: Heat and agitation cause wool to shrink [4]

paras: Merino staples are commonly 65 to 100 mm long, and wool is graded from strong (23 to 24.5 microns) to ultra-fine (11.5 to 15 microns), with finer grades generally softer [1]. Fine merino is used for next-to-skin garments because it feels less prickly than coarser wool.

Wikipedia's wool article describes wool as readily absorbing moisture, with an outer fibre surface that repels water while the interior attracts it, and notes crimped fibres that hold air and retain heat; a small study of woollen underwear linked moisture absorption to fewer heat and sweat rashes [3]. Wool ignites at a higher temperature than cotton and some synthetics, spreads flame slowly and does not melt or drip [3].
Body odour is attributed to bacteria acting on skin secretions [2]. The wool article says lanolin-treated felted wool can resist the build-up of odour [3].

Spain kept the breed under monopoly, and by the mid-16th century its wool was considered equal to the finest English wools; flocks later spread across Europe, Australia and the Americas, and Merino reached Australia in the late 18th and early 19th centuries [1]. In 2004 several retailers stopped stocking Australian merino amid a campaign against mulesing, and New Zealand banned the practice in 2018 [1].

Merino is worn as base layers, T-shirts, socks, knitwear and jackets, and wearers report wearing items several times between washes. Wikipedia's laundry article notes that heat and agitation cause wool to shrink, so garments are commonly washed gently [4].
No studies found for merino clothing specifically. The wool article mentions a small study of woollen underwear and heat and sweat rashes [3].

lore.intro: Merino is discussed in grooming and style communities as a low-odour, temperature-regulating fabric for shirts and base layers.

claims.claim: Merino wool resists odour better than synthetics.
claims.believers: Wearers say merino can be worn repeatedly without smelling, which they cite as a reason to buy it for travel and daily wear.
claims.experts: Wikipedia says lanolin-treated wool can resist odour build-up, and attributes body odour to skin bacteria; none of the sources reviewed tests merino against other fabrics [2][3].
